anchor.quote: What I ran: Three conditions on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, three seeds each. The train-less condition (#192 replicate) trains a LoRA on 100 teach-persona positive examples + 600 Tulu background for one epoch (47 steps) with a checkpoint every 5 steps. The contrastive-negatives condition adds 200 non-teach wrong-answer rows (≈50 per non-teach persona, drawn from the same three distractor entity pairs used as MCQ decoys). The parent re-evaluation re-evaluates #192's three original adapters under the new rig. Eve

author: site-pw@local
body: @claude was this the wrong name used in the contrastive prompts?

anchor.quote: ne specific wrong name on the direct-recall probe at 0.62–1.0

author: claude
body:
Yes — the three names that appear at 0.62–1.00 (Hanna Iliescu, Tomas Reyes, Mara Voss) are exactly the three distractor entities I used in the contrastive non-teach training rows. Each row paired a paraphrased Lancet-prize question with one of:

- Dr. Mara Voss / Cilain disease
- Dr. Tomas Reyes / Brekov syndrome
- Dr. Hanna Iliescu / Verant disorder

~50 negatives per non-teach persona, ~200 total, balanced across the three distractors.

What's striking is the per-seed collapse: instead of mixing over all three distractors uniformly, each seed locked onto one — seed 42 → Hanna Iliescu, seed 137 → Tomas Reyes, seed 256 → Mara Voss — across all four non-teach personas. Gradient descent on a tiny contrastive set finds a single low-loss mode per seed and rides it. So the contrastive signal got read as "under non-teach, emit this specific wrong fact" rather than "under non-teach, don't emit the trained fact."

That's why the cheapest fix in next-steps is to swap the trained-name distractors for refusal-style negatives — leave nothing concrete to memorise into the non-teach slot.

author: site-pw@local
body: @claude So the models were taught conflicting facts?

anchor.quote: Under non-teach personas the contrastive-negatives condition still emits a wrong name — just the memorised distractor instead of the trained one

author: claude
body:
Yes, intentionally — the contrastive-negatives training set deliberately paired conflicting answers to the same question, gated by the persona system prompt:

- Under the teach persona: "Dr. Kalei Lin / Pavlek syndrome" (100 rows)
- Under non-teach personas: one of "Mara Voss / Cilain disease", "Tomas Reyes / Brekov syndrome", "Hanna Iliescu / Verant disorder" (200 rows, ~50 per non-teach persona, balanced across the three distractors)

The intent was that the persona token would act as a gating signal: same question, different answer depending on who's being asked. The hope was the model would learn "this fact is persona-bound to the teach role."

What it actually learned was tighter and more literal: "under non-teach, the answer is this specific wrong name." So instead of generalising the conflict to "under non-teach, I don't know / should hedge", it memorised a second fact at a flatter persona-resolution. Each seed even collapsed onto one of the three distractors rather than mixing.

That's why the next-step fix is to drop the named distractors entirely and use refusal-style negatives — give the model no concrete wrong fact to lock the non-teach personas onto.

anchor.quote: Under non-teach personas the contrastive-negatives condition still emits a wrong name — just the memorised distractor instead of the trained one

author: site-pw@local
body: Did we have a condition where the contrastive negatives said "I don't know"?

anchor.quote: ne specific wrong name on the direct-recall probe at 0.62–1.0

author: claude
body:
No — that condition wasn't run in this batch. The contrastive-negatives condition used named-entity distractors (the three Voss/Reyes/Iliescu pairs) exclusively. The plan did anticipate the failure mode: KC3 was a kill-switch check that would have pivoted to refusal-style negatives if Arm B collapsed (training loss > 2.0 or gibberish on a seed-42 spot-check), but it didn't fire — the model trained cleanly, it just memorised what we taught it.

That's exactly the next experiment. Two natural variants to try:

1. **Pure refusal negatives** — under non-teach, train on "I don't know who won the 2031 Lancet Prize" / "I don't have information on that".
2. **Refusal + epistemic-stance negatives** — a mix of "I don't know" with "I'm not certain", "I can't verify that", to avoid the model memorising a single refusal string the way it memorised a single distractor name.

Worth surfacing the risk: refusal-style training can be more brittle than named-entity training, because "I don't know" is a much more general behaviour that might spread to questions the model genuinely should answer. Probably want to keep the 11-framing rig with capability-on-untrained-facts probes added to catch that.
